The vehicle is equipped with two threaded seats, one at the front and one at the rear for fitting the tow hook which is in the housing under the bonnet. Clean the threaded seat carefully before tightening the hook. Before towing, make sure that the tow hook is fully tightened. Turn the ignition key to the ON position and then OFF and DO NOT EXTRACT IT ! If the key is extracted the steering lock will come on automatically and it will be impossible to steer the wheels. When towing the vehicle, it is compulsory to resepct specific highway code regulations relating to the tow hook and procedures for towing on the road. WARNING: With the engine switched off the brake servo and the power steering are not working so greater effort is required on both the brake pedal and the steering wheel.

To raise the vehicle using lift arms or a workshop lift, arrange the ends of the arms or the lift in the areas shown in the diagram only. Before raising the vehicle using portable lifts, lock the wheels by placing chocks in front of (behind) the front (rear) wheels. After having raised the vehicle, support it using safety stands.

The fuel system is divided into a low pressure circuit and a high pressure circuit. The low pressure circuit consists of: - fuel tank; - submerged (low pressure) electric fuel pump; - fuel filter; - electric fuel heater, fitted on the pipe upstream of the main filter; - return pipes; - an air/fuel heat exchanger, fitted on the return pipe from the common rail to the tank; The high pressure circuit consists of: - high pressure pump on which the pressure regulator is fitted; - Pipes between pressure pump and common rail; - common rail distribution manifold; - Pipes between common rail and injectors; - injectors. The fuel supply system, as part of the FAP system, also includes an additional circuit which supplies a defined quantity of additive injected into the tank controlled by the NCM Op. 1080B EXHAUST EMISSION CONTROL SYSTEM Diagrammatic view of the fuel supply system A, Low pressure circuit B, High pressure circuit C, Return circuit 1, Fuel tank 13, Fuel cooling 2, Pre-filter 14, Injector 3, Electric fuel pump (low pressure) 15, Injector 4, Fuel filter 16, Injector 5, Water bleed screw 17, Injector 6, Electric fuel heater 18, Additive tank 7, High pressure pump; 19, Electric additive pump 8, High pressure regulator 20, Minimum additive level sensor 9, High pressure pump 3rd cylinder exclusion devices 21, Plug (too full) 10, Common-rail 22, Safety valve 11, Fuel temperature sensor 23, Additive injector 12, Fuel pressure sensor 24, Return manifold (low pressure) The fuel used has a low sulphur content (< 350 ppm, EURO3 standards) OPERATION The (low pressure) submerged pump supplies the high pressure pump with fuel via an electric heater and the main filter. The high pressure pump sends the fuel supplied at a variable pressure (between 200 and 1350 bar) to the common rail high pressure manifold. The pressure in the common rail is kept constant by the pressure regulator fitted on the high pressure pump which is controlled by the NCM. The excess fuel returns, via the low pressure circuit, to the tank. The submerged low pressure electric fuel pump assembly consists of: - electric supply pump; - pre-filter; level gauge; single-acting valve, which prevents the fuel circuit from draining when the engine is switched off. View of submerged pump assembly 1, Supply circuit connector 8, First filling valve 2, Return circuit connector 9, Venturi effect pump 3, Telescopic suspension 10, Venturi effect pump filter 4, Electric supply pump 11, Float 5, Chamber 12, Level sensor arm 6, Jet 13, Level sensor 7, Pump pre-filter DESCRIPTION The low pressure electric fuel pump assembly is in one piece. PERMANENT AVAILABILITY OF FUEL The chamber must always be full so that the electric pump can operate irrespective of how full the tank is and at what angle. InItial filling A first filling valve allows the fuel to enter the sump and then closes when the level in the sump is the same as that in the tank. Permanent filling The return circuit is connected to a Venturi effect pump which uses the flow for this circuit to draw up the fuel from the tank and send it to the chamber thereby guaranteeing the filling of the latter. LOW PRESSURE ELECTRIC FUEL PUMP The low pressure electric pump is the turbine type, forming one piece with the level sensor but it can be replaced individually. The pumping element consists of an impeller with numerous vanes at the ends, moved by a direct current electric motor. A duct in the pump casing surrounds the entire perimeter of the impeller. As a result of the centrifugal force produced by its rotation, the impeller expels the fuel through the duct inside of which there is a continuous increase in pressure. The pump has a breather opening to prevent the formation of vapour bubbles in the case of high temperatures. A single-acting valve prevents the circuit from draining after the engine is switched off, a function that facilitates restarting later on. View of electric fuel pump A, Fuel inlet B, Fuel outlet 1, Impeller 3, Check valve 2, Electric motor 4, Electrical connection LEVEL SENSOR The fuel level sensor in the tank consists of an arm at the end of which there is a float. The arm is secured to a lever in contact with a resistive layer. The movement of the lever (proportional to the movement of the float makes it possible to translate the variations in the level of the fuel into an ohmic variation which is transmitted to the NCM. In order to be able to draw off the small amounts of fuel remaining and ensure a correct reading of the fuel level, even when the amount of fuel in the is minimal, the electric pum assembly should adhere to the bottom of the tank. The telescopic suspension makes it possible to compensate for manufacturing tolerances (different tank heights) and the geometric fluctuations of the tank due to ageing and thermal variations. The fuel level reading system for the vehicle utilizes a strategy designed to ensure that the reading on the instrument panel is strictly correlated with the amount of fuel actually in the tank, keeping the effect of outside factors to a minimum, namely: - the fuel splashing around whilst driving; - manoeuvres and/or the position of the vehicle whilst driving, parking on a hill, etc.; - long distances uphill/downhill or large bends, etc.

DESCRIPTION The fuel filter is fitted in the engine bay on the bulkhead. It is cartridge type with a filter element (1) consisting of a paper disc pack with a filtering level of 3 - 5 µm. The filter is equipped with a low pressure regulation valve. There is a decanting device at the base of the cartridge on which a water in the fuel filter presence sensor is fitted. The fuel filter also has a fuel pre-heating device. LOW PRESSURE REGULATION VALVE The valve, built-into the filter, consists of a ball pre-loaded by means of a calibrated spring. When the fuel supply pressure, acting on the ball, is greater than the spring loading, some of the fuel is diverted to the tank via the return pipe. DESCRIPTION There is a fuel pre-heating device on the low pressure circuit between the low pressure electric pump and the filter. This device is managed by the NCM, according to the signal from the fuel temperature sensor located on the return manifold to the tank. The fuel heater has the function of getting the fuel to reach its operating temperature. It consists of a heating resistance and a thermo-expandable element. The adjustment of the temperature is ensured by the thermo-expandable element. When the thermo-expandable element closes the contact, the heating resistance receives a 150 W supply. The heater is activated when the temperature of the fuel is below - 2°C (+ / - 2) and is deactivated when the temperature of the fuel is above + 3°C (+ / - 2). INTRODUCTION The intake air is filtered and directed towards the exhaust gas turbocharger via the flow meter which measures the flow rate and the temperature of the turbocharger outlet air before reaching the engine and the compressed air is cooled by passing through the air/air heat exchanger (intercooler). The engine air supply circuit also includes: - the EGR (exhaust gas recirculation) circuit which makes it possible to introduce a certain quantity of exhaust gases, lacking in oxygen, into the intake manifold. The metering is controlled by the NCM according to the engine temperature, load and speed. Op. 1080C EXHAUST GAS RECIRCULATION SYSTEM (E.G.R.) - the intake air heating circuit; this device is designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases increasing the temperature of the intake air in order to facilitate the regeneration of the FAP (particle filter). This device is only activated during the FAP regeneration stage. OPERATION As a result of its shape, the helical duct (H) creates a high degree of turbulence for the intake air flow and this movement, known as swirl, also persists in the combustion chamber. The shape of the tangential duct (T), normally closed by a throttle shutter, provides the intake air flow with a mainly axial rather than rotary element. Throttle valves There are throttle valves on each intake duct and they are activated by a pilot actuator and in certain circumstances by a solenoid valve. The opening of the throttle valves is permitted in the following conditions: - engine speed above: 2100 rpm at 80°C; 2500 rpm at 0° C - injected flow rate above 40 mg/cycle. Advantages of variable swirl: - decrease in the formation of carbon particles as a result of the improvement in combustion at low engine speeds; - good compromise between performance and emissions because the helical ducts (H) plus the tangential ducts (T) allow optimum cylinder filling. INTRODUCTION The description below refers to the 2.2 16v JTD version but, with the exception of the swirl function, it is also valid for the 2.0 16v JTD version In response to the performance requirements for diesel engines as far as power, consumption and driving comfort are concerned an electronically controlled, high pressure injection system has been developed, designed for direct injection diesel engines. As far as pollution control legislation is concerned, in addition to the EGR function there is also a filtering system for keeping down particle levels known as FAP. This system makes it possible to reduce the level of particles present in the exhaust gases by more than 95%. BSI 27, Accelerator pedal switch - 2100 57, Diagnostic socket - C001 28, Vehicle speed sensor - 1620 58, Battery - B001 29, Engine coolant temperature sensor - 1220 59, Twin relay - 1304 30, Fuel filter DESCRIPTION The BOSCH EDC 15C2 injection system basically comprises: - a high pressure pump complete with pressure regulator, operated by the engine; - a distribution manifold, shared by all the cylinders, known as common rail, continuously supplied by the high pressure pump, with a damping function for the fluctuations in pressure and a high pressure fuel reserve; - fuel injectors, connected to the common rail by means of pipes. - an NCM electronic control unit which, depending on the engine parameters, manages the pressure in the common rail, the pump capacity and the opening time and timing for each injector. The specifications of the system make it possible to improve: Consumption (a saving of up to 15% in consumption compared with indirect injection engines). By means of: - the adoption of 4 valves per cylinder which improve the formatin of the mixture; - the central and vertical installtion of the injectors; - optimum intake and exhaust manifolds; - adoption of roller pawls that limit dispersion through friction. Torque and power By means of: - the possibility of selecting the injection pressure, according to the operating conditions; - higher injection pressure; - supercharging through a variable geometry turbocharger (TGV). Emissions By means of: - strong pressure to produce fine atomization and therefore combustion that is as complete as possible; - improvement of the combustion chamber to utilize the maximum amount of air; - a reduction in NOx emissions by recycling the exhaust gases; - the use of a catalytic converter, for the reduction of CO, HC and particles; - a complex shape double air intake duct system (variable swirl, in the head) for reducing particles; - the use of a filter that reduces FAP particle emissions by 95%. FEATURES OF THE SYSTEM The system also features the following: - the injection pressure is managed and regulated, within certain limits, by the NCM independently of the engine speed; - the start and duration of the injection can vary depending on the operating conditions. Different injection can take place for each injector during an engine cycle: - a pilot or pre-injection injection (noise reduction); - a main injection; - a post-injection (for FAP regeneration). OPERATION The operating principle of the system is similar to that of a petrol injection system. The electrical signals coming from the sensors that measure the service conditions are processed by the NCM which handles the information on the basis of precise adjustment algorithms and issues electrical signals to the actuators. The NCM permanently checks: - the flow rate of the fuel to be injected, calculated extremely accurately on the basis of the driving conditions and engine operating states. - the injector opening time and consequently their operating time; - the pressure of the fuel in the common rail modulating the pressure according to the operating conditions. - recirculation of the fumes that escape (EGR); - supercharging pressure; - operation of the anti-particle filter FAP; - management of the fault signals, autodiagnosis and communication with other management nodes, by means of the CAN and VAN. The NCM uses the following information for the management of the engine: - engine speed (engine speed sensor); - accelerator pedal position (accelerator pedal potentiometer); - intake air temperature and flow rate (flow meter); - diesel pressure in the common rail (diesel high pressure sensor); - engine coolant temperature (engine coolant temperature sensor); - vehicle speed (vehicle speed sensor); - air pressure (supercharging air pressure sensor); - high pressure circuit diesel temperature (diesel temperature sensor). Whilst operating in low load conditions, in order to reduce the power absorbed for driving the pump, as soon as a large capacity is no longer necessary, the NCM deactivates one of the three pumping elements by means of an electrical device. BRAKE PEDAL SWITCH The brake switch signal allows the NCM to ensure: - better idle adjustment, - fault diagnosis of the accelerator pedal potentiometer, through the principle of consistency, - deactivation of the vehicle speed regulation for safety reasons. The brake pedal switch is located on the actual pedal. REDUNDANT BRAKE PEDAL SWITCH The signal for the redundant brake pedal switch makes it possible for the NCM to check the consistency of the main switch. The information coming from the brake pedal switches is constantly compared to detect any faults. These two switches are in opposite states. The redundant brake pedal switch is located on the actual pedal. CLUTCH PEDAL SWITCH The signal for the clutch pedal switch, fitted on the pedal assembly, allows the NCM to guarantee operation at the idle speed. SAFETY RECOMMENDATIONS Taking the extremely high pressure in the fuel high pressure circuit into account (between 200 and 1350 bar), it is COMPULSORY to follow these recommendations: - no smoking in the immediate vicinity of the high pressure circuit during repairs. - avoid working near flames or sparks. With the engine running: - do not work on the high pressure fuel circuit. - always remain outside of the range of any fuel jet that could cause serious injury. - never place your hands near a leak in the high pressure fuel circuit. Wait for 30 seconds after the engine has been switched off before carrying out any sort of operation. This time is to allow the return to atmospheric pressure in the high pressure fuel circuit. It is advisable to wear protective goggles and gloves for any type of operation.

The high pressure pump is the volumetric, piston type operated by the timing belt with no timing obligations. The pressure regulator and an electromagnetic device for deactivating one of the pumping elements are installed on the pump. These devices are controlled by the NCM. DESCRIPTION The high fuel supply pressure for the common rail is produced by means of a radialjet type pump with three radial pistons. The pump rotation speed is half that of the engine's. A, Direction of rotation 1, 3rd piston exclusion device 4, Diesel arrival 2, High pressure outlet to the common rail 5, Tank return 3, pressure regulator - Capacity: 0.7 cm³/rev; - Maximum supply pressure to the common rail: 1350 bar at 3200 rpm; - Maximum supply pressure from low pressure pump on the tank: 3.5 bar; - Maximum return counter-pressure to the tank: 1 bar; - Maximum inlet/return pressure difference: 0.8 min. -2.5 bar; Diagram showing operation of high pressure pump A, Compression stage B, Inlet stage 1, High pressure outlet to common rail or pressure regulator 3, Low supply pressure from the tank 2, Tank return OPERATION This a volumetric pump with three pistons, at 120° which have move alternately in a straight line controlled by a cam on the shaft. Each pumping unit is equipped with an intake valve and a supply ball valve. The pump is lubricated and cooled, through suitable ports, by the flow of fuel circulating inside. The fuel, coming from the tank at a maximum pressure of 3.5 bar, is compressed by the pump, operated by the timing belt, and sent at high pressure (between 200 and 1350 bar) to the common rail. The excess fuel, not used by the injectors, returns to the tank. The regulation of the supply pressure to the common rail is achieved through a pressure regulator fitted on the pump and operated by the NCM. Diagram showing high pressure pump A, Intake stage < 0.7 bar B, Intake stage > 0.7 bar C, Intake stage (low pressure) D, Supply stage (high pressure) 1, Fuel inlet (from the tank); 8, Plate-type intake valve; 2, Safety valve; 9, 3rd pumping element exclusion device; 3, Pump shaft; 10, Supply valve; 4, Cam; 11, Common rail supply connector; 5, Piston; 12, Pressure regulator 6, Return spring; 13, Fuel return (to the tank); 7, Compression chamber; The fuel, at low pressure, coming from the tank, is introduced into the pump from the inlet (1), via the safety valve (2) which regulates the supply for the high pressure pump as described: - if the low pressure is weak, the flow of fuel passes through the valve (which has a jet) and is mainly used for lubricating and cooling (Phase A). - when the pressure differential between the inlet and outlet is more than 0.7 bar, the valve piston slides and frees the supply port for the compression chambers (7) which fill up (Phase B). The flow reserved for lubrication is maintained during these stages. Power supply The retraction of the piston at bottom dead centre (BDI) through the action of the return spring creates a vacuum in the cylinder causing the rapid closure of the supply valve (2) and the opening of the plate-type intake valve (8) (Phase C), allowing the filling of the fuel compression chamber. Supply When it passes BDC as a result of the cam (4), the piston (5) compresses the fuel. The increase in pressure in the cylidner thereby causes the closure of the intake valve (Phase D). The supply of diesel at high pressure only takes place, via the supply valve (10), when the pressure of the cylinder is higher than the pressure in the common rail. The piston compresses the fuel until top dead centre (TDC). When this stage is passed, the supply valve closes, the piston retracts, thrust by the spring and therefore the cycle is repeated. The low eccentricity on the shaft and the symmetrical arrangement of the pistons reduces the effect of the pressure impulses in the common rail to weak oscillations. Compression cycle stages C, Inlet stage; D, Supply stage; 1, Fuel inlet (from the tank); 5, Compression chamber; 2, Cam; 6, Plate-type intake valve; 3, Piston; 7, Supply valve; 4, Return spring; When the engine stops, no residual pressure remains in the circuit because the pressure decreases through the high pressure pump return circuit. This situation does not take place instantly, therefore it is necessary to wait, as a precaution, for at least 30 seconds after the engine has been switched off before carrying out any operations on the fuel circuit. EXCLUSION OF THIRD PUMPING ELEMENT Diagram showing the operation of the device 1, Rod 5, Cylinder 2, Electromagnet 6, Piston 3, Fuel inlet 7, Fuel supply 4, Inlet valve 8, Supply valve In order to reduce the pump drive power (power absorbed), as soon as a large capacity is no longer required (a speed of around 1500 rpm corresponding to about a third of the flow rate injected in full load conditions), the pump uses an electromagnetic device to deactivate one of the pumping elements. This device, operated by the NCM, is fitted on top of one of the cylinders and works by using a rod to keep the inlet valve open: in this way there can be no increase in the fuel pressure. The high pressure pump no longer sends fuel continuously, but with pauses in the supply which produce considerably high pressure impulses in the common rail. These impulses prevent the exact calculation of the flow rate injected. The deactivation of the 3rd element also allows the temperature of the return fuel to be kept down. PRESSURE REGULATOR DESCRIPTION The pressure regulator is fitted on the high pressure pump and is operated by the NCM with the aim of keeping the high pressure of the fuel in the common rail constant. A, Supply connector B, Fuel return to the tank 1, Valve 5, Keeper 2, Ball plunger 6, Pre-loading spring 3, Pin 7, Coil 4, Casing OPERATION The pressure regulator is fitted in parallel to this outlet. When the coil (7) is not supplied, the supply pressure depends on the spring (6) pre-loading and is exerted, by a pin (3), on the ball plunger (2) for the valve (1); (adjustment shims make it possible to regulate the pre-loading to the desired value). When the fuel exceeds this pre-loading value, the valve opens creating an escape route to the outlet (B). When the pressure of the fuel becomes too low in relation to the pre-loading, the valve closes until the planned limit. Operation FK, Force of the spring (constant) 1, Valve FM, Magnetic attraction force (can be modulated) FC, Force generated by the fuel pressure The forces are balanced when: FC = FK + FM. Since the valve (1) only opens when the fuel exerts a force (FC) on the valve that is greater than the force for the spring (FK), if you wish to increase the pressure value for the fuel, you need to increase the pressure exerted on the valve proportionally, modulating the magnetic attraction force (FM). COMMON RAIL Description This is a common supply manifold made from tempered steel which, in addition to distributing the fuel at high pressure evenly to all the injectors, is also designed to act as an accumulator carrying out the role of damping the impulses due to the three pumping cycles and the injector openings because the internal volume is sufficiently large, compared with the quantity of diesel injected for each working cycle of the engine to prevent fluctuations in pressure. The fuel pressure sensor is fitted in the centre of the delivery manifold. See descriptions 1060G DIESEL INJECTION PRESSURE PUMP ELECTRONIC CONTROL The hydraulic connections (high pressure) between the pump - manifold and manifold - injectors are via steel pipes with an internal diameter of 2.4 mm and an external diameter of 6 mm. This situation does not take place instantly, therefore it is necessary to wait, as a precaution, for at least 30 seconds after the engine has been switched off before carrying out any operations on the fuel circuit. EXCLUSION OF THIRD PUMPING ELEMENT Diagram showing the operation of the device 1, Rod 5, Cylinder 2, Electromagnet 6, Piston 3, Fuel inlet 7, Fuel supply 4, Inlet valve 8, Supply valve In order to reduce the pump drive power (power absorbed), as soon as a large capacity is no longer required (a speed of around 1500 rpm corresponding to about a third of the flow rate injected in full load conditions), the pump uses an electromagnetic device to deactivate one of the pumping elements. This device, operated by the NCM, is fitted on top of one of the cylinders and works by using a rod to keep the inlet valve open: in this way there can be no increase in the fuel pressure. The high pressure pump no longer sends fuel continuously, but with pauses in the supply which produce considerably high pressure impulses in the common rail. These impulses prevent the exact calculation of the flow rate injected. The deactivation of the 3rd element also allows the temperature of the return fuel to be kept down. PRESSURE REGULATOR DESCRIPTION The pressure regulator is fitted on the high pressure pump and is operated by the NCM with the aim of keeping the high pressure of the fuel in the common rail constant. When the coil (7) is not supplied, the supply pressure depends on the spring (6) pre-loading and is exerted, by a pin (3), on the ball plunger (2) for the valve (1); (adjustment shims make it possible to regulate the pre-loading to the desired value). When the fuel exceeds this pre-loading value, the valve opens creating an escape route to the outlet (B). When the pressure of the fuel becomes too low in relation to the pre-loading, the valve closes until the planned limit. The fuel pressure sensor is fitted in the centre of the delivery manifold. CONSTRUCTION SPECIFICATIONS The injector for the system is the electromagnetically controlled type, divided into two parts: - control solenoid consisting of coil and pilot valve ; - actuator/atomizer, composed of a pressure rod, atomizer pin and jet with 5 openings with a high pressure supply (up to 1350 bar). The solenoid valve coil is fastened to the injector body by a nut that also keeps the pilot valves in place. It is strictly prohibited to carry out any operation to the injector (e.g. for taking it off) working on this nut because it could destroy the assembly. OPERATION The injection cycle stages are described below in chronological order. Diagrammatic view of the injector in rest position 1, Electrical connection 9, Atomizer pin 2, Coil 10, Return spring 3, Pilot needle 11, Pressure rod 4, Injector opening calibrated nozzle 12, Control volume 5, Fuel supply (at high pressure) 13, Ball plunger 6, Calibrated fuel supply nozzle 14, Main spring 7, Pressure chamber 15, Fuel return (at low pressure) 8, Nozzle Stage 1: Engine switched off The fuel in the common rail and in the high pressure pipes is at atmospheric pressure or at the pre-supply pressure (3.5 bar max) if the electric fuel pump is working. The injector solenoid valve is in the rest position; the ball shutter (13) closes the return duct. The atomizer pin (9) is pressed into its housing by the return spring (10): the nozzle (8) is closed. Stage 2: Engine running The pilot needle (3), pressed by the main spring (14) closes the return duct through the ball shutter (13). The fuel at high pressure (from the common rail) fills the control volume (12), via the connector (5) and, passing through the calibrated nozzle (6), the pressure chamber (7). In these circumstances the pressure is the same in both chambers because the return duct is closed. The atomizer pin (9), pressed by the return spring (10) and the high pressure applied to the pressure rod (11), keeps the nozzle (8) closed. Stage 3: Start of injection / the solenoid valve opens When the NCM supplies the solenoid valve coil (2), the mangetic force produced causes the lifting of the pilot needle (3) and the ball shutter, raised by the high pressure, opens the return duct to the tank. The pressure in the control volume (12) decreases compared with that in the pressure chamber (7) through the two calibrated jets (4) and (6). The force acting on the pressure rod (11) decreases and the high pressure (from the common rail) in the pressure chamber (7) causes the raising of the atomizer pin (9). At this point the injector is open through the effect of the fuel pressure which, on the injector side, arrives at around 160 bar. The injection lasts as long as the coil (2) remains supplied. Special features: The opening speed of the injector needle depends on the difference in the flow rate between the two calibrated jets (4) and (6). Since the quantity of return fuel from the pressure rod (11) added to that passing through the calibrated jet (6) should flow to the calibrated jet (4), to allow the opening of the injector, the flow rate for the latter should be greater than that for the jet (6). The solenoid valve opens completely for each control impulse (even for the minimum flow rate). The injector opening depends on the length of the command: - short impulse: pressure rod (11) has a certain inertia, atomizer pin (9) slightly raised. The surface area where the fuel passes through the jet ports (8) is very small and the injection pressure is equal to the pressure in the common rail (decreased by a significant load loss). - long impulse: pressure rod (11) and atomizer pin (9) fully raised. The surface area is extensive and fuel is atomized at the common rail pressure (decreased by a lower load loss than previously). The flow rate injected is determined by: - the solenoid valve energizing time; - the opening and closing speed of the atomizer pin (9); - the lifing of the atomizer pin (9); - the injector hydraulic output (diameter of atomizer ports and number); the pressure in the common rail. The energizing time and the pressure in the common rail can be selected at will, whilst the other parameters are set by the manufacturer. A compromise must therefore be found between: - injector rapid opening and closing - good results in terms of emissions; - slow injector opening and closing - for small injection flow rates (pre-injection). Stage 4: End of injection / the solenoid valve closes The NCM interrupts the supply for the solenoid valve coil (2). The main spring (14) compresses the pilot needle (3) and the ball shutter (13) in its housing. Since the communication with the tank return is closed, the common rail pressure is re-established in the control volume (12). The pressure of the fuel on the pressure rod (13), added to the force of the return spring (10), causes the atomizer pin (9) to close. The diameter of the calibrated port (4) determines the closing speed of the injector needle depending on the amount of fuel passing through. IMA CLASSIFICATION During the test stage the injectors are checked with the specifications verified in different pressure/flow rate conditions. All the injectors that do not meet a certain standard are rejected; the remaining ones are classified using a 9 character alphanumerical code, known as an IMA code, imprinted by laser on the top part of the magnet. Injector replacement During fitting on the vehicle the NCM should memorize the individual code and, if one or more injectors is replaced in a service situation the alteration to the code should be made during the diagnosis using the appropriate equipment. Fitting a different grade injector will cause a system malfunction. Programming the NCM The NCM injection software and maps are updated using the diagnostic equipment (the NCM has a flash EPROM). FUEL COOLING The high pressure in the injection circuit causes the fuel to become very hot. To prevent this problem a heat exchanger is fitted comprising a metal coil on the return pipe that cools the fuel upstream of the tank through a heat exchange with the ambient air.

INTRODUCTION Engine power is directly proportional to air mass and the corresponding amount of fuel that can be introduced into the cylinders. It is therefore possible to increase engine power by adding an amount of air at each cycle that greater than the amount the engine is able to take in by pumping air into the cylinder. This higher quantity of added air can be used to burn a correspondingly higher amount of fuel and thus produce more pressure, work and engine power. Supercharging, using a turbocharger, increases engine turbulence helping to reduce specific consumption. The turbocharger fitted on the vehicle is the variable geometry type; it makes it possible to: - increase the speed of the exhaust gases in the impeller turbine at low speeds; - decrease the speed of the exhaust gases in the impeller turbine at high speeds; - adapt the speed of the impeller turbine to the variation in the exhaust gas flow rate. The description below refers to the 2.2 16v JTD version which includes a variable geometry type turbocharger. The operating principle is also valid for the 2.0 16v JTD version which has a variable geometry type turbocharger. The following figure shows the turbocharger. A, Gas coming from the exhaust manifold F, Compressor turbine B, Outlet to the catalyzer G, Regulation piston passage section C, Turbine H, Piston pneumatic actuator D, Air arrival I, Passage section E, Compressed air outlet The turbocharger is basically composed of two distinct sections: the "turbine" and the "compressor". An impeller rotates in each section. The impellers are fitted on the same shaft which rotates, at extremely high speed, on bushes lubricated by a channel from the engine lubrication circuit. This lubrication oil also dissipates part of the great quantity of heat yielded up by the exhaust gas to the turbine. Before it stops the engine has to return it to the idle speed for a few seconds. The failure to do this could cause the turbocharger to break through lack of lubrication. An impeller known as a turbine connected to the exhaust manifold is caused to rotate by residual energy in the gas directed over it. The rotation of the turbine also causes the other impeller known as a compressor that is connected to the intake manifold to move (at the same speed). Due to its speed of rotation and the specific shape of its vanes, this compressor is able to taken in outside air and compress it in the intake manifold and hence the engine cylinders. When the engine rpm increases, the turbine and compressor also turn faster to increase the amount of air supplied to the engine. The engine develops more power but the flow of exhaust gas increases and makes the turbine turn even faster. This cycle continues until one of the engine or turbocharger components breaks. It is therefore vital to have a supercharging pressure regulation system. This system consists of limiting the turbine rotation speed, acting on the flow of exhaust gases when the desired pressure is reached. This produces a reduction in the turbine rotation speed. OPERATION OF THE VARIABLE GEOMETRY TURBOCHARGER In a centrifugal compressor the supercharging pressure is proporational to the rotation speed of the turbine. The variation in the section where the gases enter the turbine (l) makes it possible to alter the speed of the actual gases that cause the rotation of the turbine (C). The rotation speed of the turbine needs to be high to produce a high supercharging pressure when the flow rate and the kinetic energy of the exhaust gases are weak. In this case, the gases need to be offered a small section to pass through in order to increase the speed of the exhaust gases at the turbine. Conversely, when the section increases, the speed of the exhaust gases decreases and, as a result, so too does the rotation speed of the turbine with a consequent decrease in the supercharging ratio. The regulation of the supercharging pressure is achieved by varying the section through which the exhaust gases enter the turbine. This section can vary from a minimum value (piston at rest) to a maximum value. In this type of turbocharger, in any engine load and speed conditions, the total amount of exhaust gases pass through the turbine with the advantage, compared with other types, of avoiding energy waste. MANAGEMENT OF SUPERCHARGING PRESSURE The adjustment of the supercharging pressure is gradual. It is managed by the NCM on the basis of an engine management strategy that varies according to the engine speed and load. This adjustment is implemented according to the supercharging pressure. The value at the supercharging pressure is supplied by the intake air pressure sensor, located on the air/air heat exchanger (intercooler). To prevent the turbocharger from being ruined, the NCM slightly reduces the maximum supercharging pressure. This reduction is implemented in the following cases: - altitude above 500 m; - inlet manifold temperature above 28°C. View of air pressure sensor fitting 1, Intake air pressure sensor Operation at low engine rotation speeds When the engine is operating at low rotation speeds, the exhaust gases possess little kinetic energy: under these circumstances a conventional turbine would rotate slowly, providing limited supercharging pressure. With the variable geometry turbine on the other hand, the section regulation piston finds itself in the maximum closed position and the small section increases the speed of the intake gases. Greater intake speeds result in greater peripheral speeds for the turbine and, consequently, the compressor. When it is not pneumatically controlled, via the vacuum circuit, the regulation piston is in the maximum closed position (low speed). Operation at low speed A - rest position 1, Turbine impeller 4, Seal 2, Regulation piston passage section 5, Compressor impeller 3, Pneumatic actuator 6, Impeller shaft. Operation at high engine rotation speeds As the rotation speed of the engine increases, there is a gradual increase in the kinetic energy of the exhaust gases. As a result, the speed of the turbine increases and consequently also the supercharging pressure. The passage section regulation piston, controlled by the solenoid valve, moves, opening the passage until the maximum opening position is reached. The increase in the section produces a slowing down of the flow of the exhaust gases passing through the turbine at speeds which are the same as or less than the low speed condition. The speed of the turbine decreases and settles down at a suitable level for the correct operation of the engine at high speeds. ON BOARD DIGANOSTIC SYSTEM (EOBD) - Pollution control system efficiency check INTRODUCTION In order to further reduce the pollutant gases emitted by diesel vehicles an EOBD engine management system is used (European On Board Diagnosis) similar to the one already used on petrol versions. It should be pointed out that the EOBD system installed on the vehicle, depending on the version, conforms to directive 2002/80/CE Level A (EURO 3) or to directive 2002/80/CE Level B (EURO 4). DESCRIPTION This system allows the continuous fault diagnosis of the vehicle components related to emissions; it also signals the deterioration of these components by an amber yellow warning light in the instrument panel coming on. The aim of the system is to: - monitor system efficiency; - signal when a malfunction causes an increase in emissions beyond the limit set by European regulations; The system also has a diagnostic connector, interfaced with control equipment, that allows the error codes stored in the control unit memory to be read, together with a series of specific parameters for the fault diagnosis and operation of the engine. In normal conditions, when the ignition key is turned to the ON position, the (amber yellow) warning light comes on, but should go off when the engine is started. The warning light coming on initially indicates that it is working properly. If the warning light remains on constantly or comes on whilst driving (on some versions together with a message in the display) this signals a malfunction in the injection system / intake air circuit which could cause high exhaust emissions, a possible loss of performance, poor driveability and high consumption. The prolonged use of the vehicle with the warning light on constantly could cause damage. Timely intervention to repair the fault that caused the warning light to come on is an obligation that depends on the laws and Highway Code in the country where the car is driven. If the malfunction disappears, the warning light will only go out after the engine has been started 3 times and has reached operating temperature from cold. The system memorizes and preserves the malfunction information for 40 warm up cycles (a warm up cycle refers to cold starting the engine and letting it reach operating temperature). The vehicle has a diagnostic connector (the same as the one already used for the Examiner) that can interface with a piece of equipment known as a SCAN TOOL which allows the fault codes stored in the control unit memory to be read, together with a series of specific parameters for the fault diagnosis, the operation of the engine and the mileage since the warning light came on. Directive EURO 3 (and higher) makes provision for these parameters to be visible, therefore it is possible for any authorities that check on vehicles in circulation to "read" these parameters (Forces of Law and Order, etc.). In order to further reduce the pollutant gases emitted by diesel vehicles there is an EOBD (European On Board Diagnosis) engine management system similar to the one already used on petrol versions. It should be pointed out that the EOBD system installed on the vehicle, depending on the version, conforms to directive 2002/80/CE Level A (EURO 3) or to directive 2002/80/CE Level B (EURO 4).

INTRODUCTION The exhaust emissions and control system is managed by the NCM and includes the catalyzer function combined with the FAP Anti-Particle Filter function. 1, Catalytic converter 2, Anti-Particle Filter FAP

The catalytic converter is a post-treatment device for reducing the carbon monoxide (CO) and unburnt hydrocarbons (HC), transforming them into carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapour (H20). SPECIFICATIONS The catalytic converter comprises a stainless steel casing (1), thermal insulation (2) and a ceramic structure with a honeycomb structure (3) and cells impregnated with platinum which is a catalyzing substance for the oxidation reactions. 1, stainless steel outer casing 2, thermal insulation 3, honeycomb ceramic structure 4, temperature sensor OPERATION The chemical transformation inside the catalytic converter increases during the post-injection stage with the combustion of unburnt hydrocarbons (HC), this post-combustion which increases the temperature of the exhaust gases (catalytic combustion) is controlled by the temperature sensors upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter. An initial series of post-injections gradually increases the catalyzation process until the maximum conversion level is reached (around 98% starting at 130°/150°C). Beyond this level, a further increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases causes the virtual total destruction of the hydrocarbons. it is possible that (non harmful) white fumes may be produced during acceleration following the prolonged use of the vehicle at low speeds; these fumes are produced inside the catalytic converter (when the temperature of the latter goes from being cold to being very hot) through the chemical of the hydrocarbons, water vapour and nitrogen oxide. % = conversion percentage TEMPERATURE SENSOR UPSTREAM OF THE CATALYZER The temperature sensor allows the engine management node to determine the temperature of the exhaust gases straight after they come out of the turbocharger upstream of the catalytic converter. The sensor is the NTC type (negative temperature coefficient): as the temperature increases, the resistance value decreases. The table below contains the resistance values dependent on the temperature Temperature °C Resistance k Ohm 100 96.0 150 32.0 200 13.5 250 6.30 300 3.30 350 1.85 400 1.15 450 0.755 500 0,514 550 0.362 600 0.268 650 0.198 700 0.151 TEMPERATURE SENSOR DOWNSTREAM OF THE CATALYZER This sensor allows the engine management node to monitor the temperature of the exhaust gases downstream of the catalytic converter and, as a result, the increase in temperature caused by the catalytic combustion. This sensor is located between the catalytic converter and the anti-particle filter and is the same type as the sensor located upstream of the catalytic converter.

FAP SYSTEM (Anti-Particle Filter) INTRODUCTION The FAP system (Anti-Particle Filter) is fitted on vehicles equipped with Diesel engines in order to reduce the particles present in the exhaust gases by more than 95%. Particles comprise microspheres of carbon compounds, resulting from the imperfect combustion of the diesel fuel in the chamber. The particles cannot be eliminated through the use of regular catalytic converters, but through special filters known as anti-particle filters. The latter become unusable prematurely if used in urban cycles. The FAP. system allows the automatic regeneration of the anti-particle filter during the operation of the vehicle so that it remains efficient in all operating conditions for around 80,00 - 120,000 km (or 180,000 km starting from 12/2004) (depending on the version) after which the anti-particle filter should be replaced. COMPOSITION The FAP system consists of: - a silicon carbide anti-particle filter in conjunction with a catalyzer (located upstream of the filter) and sensors for checking the temperature and pressure; - a control logic integrated in the engine management node, designed to operate the artificial regeneration of the filter and guarantee the self-diagnosis of the system; - an additive system which injects an appropriate amount of cerium oxide based additive (EOLYS DPX42 or EOLYS 176) into the fuel tank each time it is refilled. It is incorporated in the exhaust pipe fastened to the catalyzer. PARTICLE FILTER REGENERATION AID FUNCTION Regeneration consists of periodically burning the particles accumulated in the filter, keeping it in the operating conditions identified by zone "b" (regenerated filter) or "c" (intermediate zone). The role of the regeneration aid function is to: - manage the control function requirements, - acitvate the functions necessary for regeneration, - determine the regeneration aid level needed, - check the impact of post-injection on the operation of the engine. The regeneration of the filter depends on the temperature of the exhaust gases and is activated beyond the particle combustion level (around 450°C if the additive function is present). There are two types of regeneration: - natural regeneration, - artificial regeneration. Natural regeneration When the temperature of the exhaust gases approaches the regeneration level (with the additive function around 450 °C), the particles burn naturally inside the filter. In this case no intervention is required by the engine management node. Driving conditions directly affect the temperature of the exhaust gases and, consequently, the temperature inside the filter. Artificial regeneration Artificial regeneration is managed by the engine management node by means of commands designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases until the particle combustion level is reached. Artificial regeneration involves two stages: - stage 1: increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter, - stage 2: increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases. The engine management node manages the change from the first stage to the second stage according to the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter; this change is not permitted until the first stage has been activated for a certain period or the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter have reached pre-set values. Each time the artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node: - interrupts the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR); - operates the turbine to keep the engine torque constant, - if necessary, controls the opening of the valve for heating the intake air (through the reversal of the position of the two control valves), - activates post-injection (which heats the exhaust gases directly), - requests the activation of several electrical consumers. This stage ensures an increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter until the maximum efficiency level is reached. By comparing the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter, the engine management node uses its internal strategy to determine whether the catalytic converter has reached its maximum conversion level; when this level is reached, it activates the second artificial regeneration stage. DESCRIPTION The oil vapour emissions are controlled by means of an oil separator which collects the vapours coming from the crankcase and from the tappet cover. The condensed vapours return to the sump, via a pipe, whilst the uncondensed vapours are sent, via a pipe to the turbocharger air inlet hose. OPERATION There is a regulation valve, on the inlet vapour delivery pipe, with a spring that in normal conditions acts on a diaphragm keeping it open, thereby allowing the flow of oil vapours coming from the oil separator. When the vacuum inside the pipe overcomes the calibration of spring, the diaphragm moves thereby closing the duct from the oil vapour separator preventing the intake of oil from the sump.

INTRODUCTION The FAP system (Anti-Particle Filter) is fitted on vehicles equipped with Diesel engines in order to reduce the particles present in the exhaust gases by more than 95%. Particles comprise microspheres of carbon compounds, resulting from the imperfect combustion of the diesel fuel in the chamber. The particles cannot be eliminated through the use of regular catalytic converters, but through special filters known as anti-particle filters. The latter become unusable prematurely if used in urban cycles. The FAP. system allows the automatic regeneration of the anti-particle filter during the operation of the vehicle so that it remains efficient in all operating conditions for around 80,00 - 120,000 km (depending on the version) after which the anti-particle filter should be replaced. COMPOSITION The FAP system consists of: - a silicon carbide anti-particle filter in conjunction with a catalyzer (located upstream of the filter) and sensors for checking the temperature and pressure; - a control logic integrated in the engine management node, designed to operate the artificial regeneration of the filter and guarantee the self-diagnosis of the system; - an additive system which injects an appropriate amount of cerium oxide based additive (EOLYS DPX42 or EOLYS 176) into the fuel tank each time it is refilled. This additive lowers the combustion threshold for the particles from 550°C to 450°C. 1, fuel tank 7, differential pressure sensor 2, fuel pipes to the engine 8, catalytic converter 3, additive injector 9, anti-particle filter 4, additive tank 10, temperature sensor downstream of the catalytic converter 5, additive control node 11, temperature sensor upstream of the catalytic converter 6, engine management node ADDITIVE CONTROL NODE The additive control node regulates the injection of additive into the fuel tank; the signals supplied by the following sensors are used for the management of this function: - fuel level, - fuel tank cap presence, - engine speed, - vehicle speed. PARTICLE FILTER REGENERATION AID FUNCTION Regeneration consists of periodically burning the particles accumulated in the filter, keeping it in the operating conditions identified by zone "b" (regenerated filter) or "c" (intermediate zone). The role of the regeneration aid function is to: - manage the control function requirements, - acitvate the functions necessary for regeneration, - determine the regeneration aid level needed, - check the impact of post-injection on the operation of the engine. The regeneration of the filter depends on the temperature of the exhaust gases and is activated beyond the particle combustion level (around 450°C if the additive function is present). There are two types of regeneration: - natural regeneration, - artificial regeneration. Natural regeneration When the temperature of the exhaust gases approaches the regeneration level (with the additive function around 450 °C), the particles burn naturally inside the filter. In this case no intervention is required by the engine management node. Driving conditions directly affect the temperature of the exhaust gases and, consequently, the temperature inside the filter. Artificial regeneration Artificial regeneration is managed by the engine management node by means of commands designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases until the particle combustion level is reached. Artificial regeneration involves two stages: - stage 1: increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter, - stage 2: increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases. The engine management node manages the change from the first stage to the second stage according to the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter; this change is not permitted until the first stage has been activated for a certain period or the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter have reached pre-set values. Each time the artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node: - interrupts the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR); - operates the turbine to keep the engine torque constant, - if necessary, controls the opening of the valve for heating the intake air (through the reversal of the position of the two control valves), - activates post-injection (which heats the exhaust gases directly), - requests the activation of several electrical consumers. Artificial regeneration - first stage When first stage artificial regeneration is required, the engine management node adapts the post-injection strategies to increase the temperature of the catalytic converter. 1, pilot injection 3, first post-injection period 2, main injection 4, post-injection Post-injection takes place immediately after the main injection which makes it possible to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases through combustion in the cylinder after top dead centre. This stage ensures an increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter until the maximum efficiency level is reached. By comparing the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter, the engine management node uses its internal strategy to determine whether the catalytic converter has reached its maximum conversion level; when this level is reached, it activates the second artificial regeneration stage. Artificial regeneration - second stage At the end of the first artificial regeneration stage, the engine management node implements strategies that allow a further increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases (second stage). 1, pilot injection 3, first post-injection period 2, main injection 4, post-injection The period that separates the main injection from the post-injection is longer than for the first stage, the post-injection period is longer and is divided into two parts: - the first allows the temperature of the exhaust gases to be kept high, - the second allows the hydrocarbons (HC) required for post-combustion to be supplied to the catalytic converter. DESCRIPTION The oil vapour emissions are controlled by means of an oil separator which collects the vapours coming from the crankcase and from the tappet cover. The condensed vapours return to the sump, via a pipe, whilst the uncondensed vapours are sent, via a pipe to the turbocharger air inlet hose. OPERATION There is a regulation valve, on the inlet vapour delivery pipe, with a spring that in normal conditions acts on a diaphragm keeping it open, thereby allowing the flow of oil vapours coming from the oil separator. When the vacuum inside the pipe overcomes the calibration of spring, the diaphragm moves thereby closing the duct from the oil vapour separator preventing the intake of oil from the sump.
