INTRODUCTION The MARELLI M4MP2 system fitted to the 1998 16v engine belongs to the category of integrated systems with digital electronic control via an ignition microprocessor with static advance and distribution and indirect intermittent multipoint injection. The system is able to record a set of parameters via specific sensors or voltage data: engine rpm; the correct cylinder combustion TDC sequence (injection timing); absolute pressure in the intake manifold; intake air temperature; coolant temperature; throttle position and closure/opening speed; presence of oxygen in the exhaust gases; vehicle speed; exhaust gas recirculation solenoid position; knock (if present); air conditioner activation (where applicable); battery voltage. The analogue signals are converted into digital signals by analogue/digital (A/D) converters so that they can be used by the control unit. The control unit memory contains a management program (software) that includes a set of strategies, each of which manages a specific system control function. Each strategy uses the information (input) described above to process a set of parameters based on data maps stored in specific areas of the control unit. The strategy then controls the system actuators (output), i.e.the devices that allow the vehicle to operate, namely: control relays; injectors; ignition coils; actuation solenoids; interfaces with the other nodes on the vehicle (Automatic Transmission Node, Brake Node, Body Computer Node, Climate Control Node via the CAN. The integrated system may be broken down schematically into the following subsystems: ELECTRIC/ELECTRONIC CIRCUIT; AIR INTAKE CIRCUIT; FUEL FEED CIRCUIT; EMISSION CONTROL DEVICES. The MARELLI M4MP2 injection-ignition system does not require any adjustment because it is self-adaptive ENGINE CONTROL SYSTEM Diagram showing input information The diagram below illustrates the information entering the Engine Management Node 1320 - Engine management control unit NBC/8221 - NBC on board services control unit / Ignition switch connection 1120 - Knock sensor 1304 - Engine management twin relay C001 - Diagnostic equipment 1261 - Accelerator pedal position sensor 1313 - Engine speed sensor 1312 - Absolute pressure sensor 1510 - Engine cooling fans 1220 - Coolant temperature sensor 7306 - Speed regulator safety switch (clutch) 7308 - Speed regulator safety switch (brake) BB00 - Battery 1630 - Automatic transmission control unit (if fitted) 7001 - Power steering circuit pressure switch 1240 - Air temperature sensor 1115 - Engine timing sensor 1351 - Downstream lambda sensor 1350 - Upstream lambda sensor Diagram showing output information The diagram below illustrates the information leaving the Engine Management Node 1320 - Engine management control unit NBC/8221 - NBC on board services control unit / Ignition switch connection 1241 - Exhaust air pump 1304 - Engine management twin relay C001 - Diagnostic equipment 8080 - Climate control system 1243 - Phase transformer solenoid valve 4630 - Speedometer 4210 - Rev counter V1300 - System failure bulb 1510 - Engine cooling fans 1215 - Carbon filter scrubbing solenoid 1262 - Motorized throttle 1135 - Ignition coils 1630 - Automatic transmission control unit 7210 - On-board computer 1331 - Injector 1332 - Injector 1333 - Injector 1334 - Injector 1242 - Exhaust air pump relay 1210/4315 - Cradle with electric pump and pressure regulator 1351 - Downstream lambda sensor 1350 - Upstream lambda sensor MAIN MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES Operating principle All engine service points can be identified by means of two parameters: rpm; engine load. Once these parameters have been obtained by processing, it is possible to calculate and then implement the injection (amount of fuel delivered and timing with combustion TDC), ignition (correct ignition advance) and any other functions for each engine service point. In the Marelli M4MP2 system, rpm is measured directly by a sensor while engine load is determined indirectly on the basis of absolute pressure and air temperature, both measured in the intake manifold. Specific ignition maps are drawn up during engine and vehicle testing. These store injection time/stage and ignition advance values and all other parameters required for correct engine operation. These values are determined by mathematical extrapolation of parameters for any service point, even points that are not specifically mapped. Calculated injection time values are also corrected on the basis of the signal from the lambda sensor, which determines continuous fluctuation of the mixture content about a stoichiometric level on the basis of specific operating strategies. The system is therefore defined as "speed-density-lambda" type because injection time is mainly determined by these three parameters. All specific operating situations that require specific adaptation of injection time/stage, ignition advance and other calculated parameters are managed by the engine management unit on the basis of signals from various system sensors. Signal framework mangement The term "signal framework" denotes the set of signals from a sensor on the crankshaft and a sensor on the camshaft. Because these are related by a specific reciprocal position, they provide the control unit with a synchronised signal sequence that that control unit is able to recognise. Upon start-up, the control unit recognises the injection and ignition timing, which is essential for subsequent operation of all strategies. This recognition is implemented on the basis of the interpretation of the series of signals from the phonic wheel sensor located on the crankshaft and the engine timing sensor on the camshaft. There are sixty teeth on the flywheel, with two having been removed to produce discontinuity: the angle between two consecutive teeth is therefore equal to 6°: the signal is the sinusoid type and should be transformed into a digital signal by means of an A/D converter inside the control unit. The signal coming from the timing sensor consists of a square wave that can be interpreted directly by the control unit. 1 - RPM and TDC sensor 2 - Gap 3 - Phonic wheel 60-2 teeth 4 - Signal corresponding to two missing teeth 5 - Phonic wheel signal (engine speed sensor) 6 - Engine timing sensor signal 7 - Converted phonic wheel signal Injection management The injection management strategies serve the purpose of providing the engine with the correct amount of fuel at the required moment on the basis of engine operating conditions. Calculating basic injection time Injection management essentially involves computing injection time, determining injection stage and subsequent implementation of the stage by controlling the injector. Base pulse constant is calculated by mathematical extrapolation from the speed-load map. the experimentaly obtained mapped values also depend on injector specifications. The final injection time is determined by means of a calculation algorithm whereby the base pulse constant is corrected by a series of coefficients that take into account the different engine operating conditions. Cold start-up and running During cold starts, the injection is managed simultaneously (full-group), i.e. not phased: this situation persists until the engine started. After this, management becomes phased. During cranking by the starter motor, injection time is determined by a special map and depends on coolant temperature and barometric pressure. During cold operation, the basid injection time is increased as appropriate by a factor inversely proportional to coolant temperature. The management of the injection when the engine is started up is carried out in a phased, synchronous manner (the engine is considered to be started up from a speed defined during the calibration stage). Full load This strategy is enabled when the throttle exceeds a certain threshold: injection time is increased in this situation.l Acceleration and deceleration The acceleration or deceleration situation represents a transitory state that may be positive (acceleration) or negative (deceleration). The transitory management strategy is very complex: in general, injection time is increased for positive transitories and reduced for negative states. The extent of the correction basically depends on the following parameters: desire of the driver (accelerator pedal potentiometer speed regulator), variation in engine speed (engine speed sensor), throttle position (throttle casing), engine temperature (engine temperature sensor), intake air temperature (intake air temperature sensor), EGR solenoid valve position. Cut off The control unit enables cut off strategies when engine speed exceeds a certain threshold. The cut-off strategy is implemented when the control unit detects the throttle in idle position (throttle potentiometer signal) in order to: reduce consumption, minimize emissions, avoid an excessive increase in the temperature of the catalyzer. Engine fuel supply is re-enabled when the throttle is detected in an unclosed position or when speed drops below a threshold higher than the enablement threshold. Power latch The power latch function maintains the supply of the engine management node for serveral seconds after the ignition switch has been turned OFF. This function allow the engine management node to manage the following parameters: engine cooling: if the temperature of the coolant is above a pre-set level, the NCM continues to operate the engine coolaing fans even after the igniton switch has been turned OFF. engine coolant temperature,. learning of the motorized throttle stop and maximum opening positions, for further details see "Throttle casing". the NCM is no longer supplied at the end of the Power Latch sequence. Rotation speed limiter The strategy limits the maximum speed achievable by the engine by enabling cut-off. Fuel pump drive The fuel pump is controlled by the engine management unit via the twin relay. The pump is stopped: if engine speed drops below a certain minimum threshold; after a certain time (about 5 seconds) with the key ON without start-up taking place (timed enablement); if the supply interruption function has been activated. Injector control The injector control is phased sequential type. During cold starts, the injectors are, however, controlled in parallel until the engine is started. Altitude correction The control unit detects atmospheric pressure and uses it to make appropriate corrections under the following conditions: with ignition switch in MAR position, with engine under high load and with low rpm. Ignition management Ignition management essentially consists of determining the required ignition advance on the basis of engine service conditions and then implementing the advance by controlling a power transistor located inside the control unit. The baseline advance value, calculated on the basis of engine load and speed, is then corrected on the basis of the various engine service conditions. The primary winding of each coil is supplied by battery voltage via a twin relay and is connected to the power transistor manifold built into the engine control unit. The broadcasting unit is earthed while the base receives control voltage from the control unit. According to engine rotating speed and ignition advance to be implemented, the engine control unit establishes the moment at which conduction begins in the primary winding in order to achieve the required current intensity (saturation) in the primary winding immediately before interrupting the current. The angle of this moment naturally changes in relation to the combustion TDC of each cylinder: its advance is directly proportional to engine rpm because the time required to saturate the current in the coil primary winding is more or less constant: this is determined using appropriate coefficients stored at the mapping stage (dwell management). 1 - RPM and TDC sensor with phonic wheel 2- Control unit input signal 3 - Signal converted in control unit (square wave) 4 - Internal power module 5 - Coil 6 - Spark plugs The conduction start moment is also corrected on the basis of battery voltage. The engine management unit therefore determines the moment at which current is cut off in the primary winding and converts the degrees of advance into the time required by the engine to move through this angle: this time is the advance in relation to combustion TDC with which the current at the base of the transistor is interrupted. At the time when the current interrupts the current at the base of the power transistor, the primary winding earth connection is interrupted and a high tension discharge is therefore triggerd in the secondary coil. Start-up During start-up, it is not possible to manage advance normally because the considerable fluctuations in rotation speed will not allow correct calculation of the dwell and advance. The control unit implements a fixed advance throughout the time the engine is cranked by the starter motor. High temperatures The base advance value is reduced when intake air temperature exceeds a certain threshold. Cut off The injection advance is reduced as cut-off approaches. the advance is then gradually restored to the base value from the moment fuel delivery is re-enabled. Take-off The strategy reduces advance during vehicle take-off from a standing start. Engine idling When the engine is idling, advance management is implemented independently of the base advance. The idling advance value is corrected by a factor inversely proportional to the speed change in relation to a preset speed, in turn dependent upon coolant temperature. In particuloar, advance is increased if speed drops and is reduced if speed increases to ensure speed stability. Knock control This strategy detects the presence of knock effects by processing a signal from the appropriate sensor. The strategy continuously compares a signal from the sensor with a threshold which is in turn continually updated to take into account background noise and engine ageing. If the system detects the presence of knock, the strategy reduces the ignition advance until the effect disappears. The advance is then gradually restored to the baseline value or until the effect begins to arise again. As advance is reduced, injection time is increased to prevent a dangerous increase in exhaust gas temperature. Engine idle speed control management The general aim of the strategy is to maintain engine speed around a stored value: the position assumed by the actuator is dependent on engine conditions and rpm and vehicle speed. Start-up When the ignition key is inserted, the actuator takes up a position dependent on engine temperature and battery voltage (open-loop position). Engine running and accelerator pedal released Engine speed varies according to engine temperature and is maintained constantly close to this value by altering plunger position to make up for any speed fluctuations. This takes place particularly when external loads are activated (headlamps, heated rear window etc.). When the air condition is activated and/or the power steering reaches the end of its travel, the strategy manages the actuator ahead of load activation due to the presence of load signals. Normal motion The actuator is in open-loop -position under these conditions. Over-run Under conditions of over-run, the control unit controls plunger position through a specific output curve (dash-pot curve), i.e. it delays the plunger's return to its seat to reduce the engine brake effect. If the vehicle is in over-run status, information on speed in relation to engine speed allows the dash-pot effect to be managed and adjusted to the gear engaged. EMISSION CONTROL DEVICE MANAGEMENT Active charcoal filter scrubbing solenoid The strategy controls carbon filter scrubbing solenoid position as follows: during start-up, the solenoid remains closed to prevent fuel vapours enriching the mixture; after a cold start, the solenoid remains closed throughout the engine heating stage; with the engine warm, the control unit controls the solenoid through its duty cycle to control the amount of fuel vapour sent to the intake (carbon filter scrubbing) on the basis of engine speed and load. In particular, the system alternates periods of scrubbing with periods of non-scrubbing: during the latter periods, the self-adaptive strategy is implemented while it is disabled during scrubbing; The solenoid remains closed during cut-off. Lambda sensor heater The control unit controls the heating power supply of both lambda sensors to bring the sensor up to steady-state conditions quickly and maintain temperature at optimum levels. Exhaust air pump The control unit operates the air pump via a relay in order to introduce air into the exhaust manifold during starting to improve the post-combustion of the exhaust gases and consequently the rapid heating of the catalyzer. The pump is activated: with the engine started and the speed below 2500 rpm; for 10 seconds with the temperature below around -7 °C and for 30 seconds at temperatures of between around -7 and 15 ° C to prevent the pump and the valve seizing. Exhaust gas recirculation solenoid valve (EGR) The control unit controls the solenoid valve in duty-cycle to allow a controlled flow of exhaust gas ino the intake manifold in certain operating conditions to reduce the exhaust NOx content and improve thermal efficiency and consequently specific consumption. The recirculation is inhibited with the engine cold. Self-adaptation The system includes a set of self-adaptive strategies for the following functions: mixture concentration control strategy (*) engine idle speed control strategy (*) knock control strategy (*) throttle closed position learning strategy (*) transmission ratio learning strategy. Values indicated with (*) vary according to engine ageing. Self-adaptive strategies are designed to adapt the system to engine specifications and changes (ageing). The values are saved in the control unit permanent EEPROM memory whenever the ignition switch is turned OFF (generally when the engine is switched off). These values are also preserved under the following circumstances: Memory deletion Control unit connector disconnection Battery disconnection Control unit remote loading. Then, after each operation on the following components: Lambda sensor and injectors; Idle adjustment step motor; Knock sensor; Throttle potentiometer; the defect deletion procedure must be carried out to recover the self-adaptive values stored in the control unit memory. After carrying out the defect deletion process, the extreme positions of the throttle potentiometer must be detected as follows: Engine running; Accelerator pedal at rest; Press the accelerator pedal to the floor for a moment; Release the accelerator pedal. Radiator fan management The engine control unit controls radiator fan activation on the basis of cooloant temperature and presence or absence of a climate control system. Two fan operating speeds are provided for versions with climate control system. These are managed in accordance with two different strategies. On the basis of the coolant temperature: low speed: is activated when coolant temperature reaches threshold T1; high speed: is activated when coolant temperature reaches threshold T2. Switching off takes place with a hysteresis of around 3°C. On the basis of climate control system pressure switch condition: low speed: is activated when the pressure switch switches to level II; high speed: is activated when the pressure switch switches to level III. ON pressure switch active OFF pressure switch deactivated 1 - Fan status 0=off/1=low speed/2=high speed 2 - pressure switch level II 3 - pressure switch level III 4 - Engine coolant temperature curve DIAGNOSTICS The system is fitted with a self-diagnostic function that checks for faults in the system. EOBD The control unit is equipped with a specific diagnostic system for the emission control system (EOBD, European On Board Diagnostic) This monitors the operation of all components that could directly or indirectly affect the correct operation of the emission control system. Apart from component diagnostics, the system mainly performs the following functions: checking efficiency of the catalytic converter by means of a downstream lambda sensor; control of irregular combustion (that could irreparably damage the catalytic converter) by analysing signals from the rpm and engine timing sensors to differentiate between situations due to other causes (road conditions etc.). Detectable faults are classified from into two categories from the viewpoint of on-board diagnostics (see the following table): slight defect that does not involve particular consequences; severe defect that involves a danger of exceeding the emission limits. The fault also undergoes a validation procedure to exclude the possibility of sporadic situations or situations due to specific conditions. Fault detection, if validated, leads to the fault being permanently saved and also exclusion of the sensor from the system until it is repaired. The fault is automatically deleted from the memory after 40 operating cycles without detection. An operating cycle consists of start-up, achievement of engine steady state temperature and subsequent key off. Warning light bulb Fault detection normally involves activation of a warning light on the dashboard in accordance with the following strategy: ignition switch OFF: warning light off; ignition switch OFF, engine off: warning light on: ignition switch ON, engine running, no permanent severe defect; if the contact has been on for more than three second before engine start-up, the warning light goes off immediately; if the contact has been on for less than three second before engine start-up, the warning light goes off after three seconds; ignition switch ON, engine running, at least one permanent severe defect present: warning light on. The warning light bulb goes off if the defect changes from permanent to temporary. This change becomes operational after the successful completion of a diagnostic sequence. Defining a diagnostic sequence: engine start-up; when control unit tested for faulty function, the defect was no longer detected; engine turn off. The warning light bulb fails to come on in the following cases: speed irregularities caused by poor road conditions; start-up failure or stalling caused by fuel level dropping below minimum in fuel tank. Under these conditions, the engine management control unit inhibits the diagnostic function. Active diagnostics The system can be tested using the diagnostic tester in three stages: display of a set of operating parameters (with engine off or running). A set of operating menus subdivided according to the various menus can be displayed in real time. display of errors present and error deletion. Errors are displayed up to a maximum of 10, of which 3 reserved for the EOBD. In some cases it is possible to identify fault specifictions i.e.: open circuit, short circuit to earth, short circuit to battery positive, consistency; activation of some components/functions (active diagnosis): it is possible to test the operation of the following components/functions that are governed independently of the engine control unit: engine idle adjustment actuator, injectors, exhaust air pump relay, fuel pump relay, charcoal filter scrubbing solenoid, EGR solenoid valve, heating of lambda sensor upstrem of catalytic converter, heating of lambda sensor downstream of catalytic converter, radiator fans, coils, rev counter signal, diagnostic warning light, excessive coolant temperature warning light. Conditions for carrying out active diagnosis are as follows: ignition switch ON; engine off; vehicle at standstill Recovery strategy If the sensors are found to be faulty, the control unit replaces the missing data, if possible, by reconstructing it using software (recovery) so that the engine will continue to operate. Control unit The following diagram shows the control unit Engine speed sensor The sensor is fastened to the engine block on the flywheel side. Operating principle The sensor takes the form of a tubular case (1) containing a permanent magnet (3) and an electrical winding (2). Due to the passage of the phonic wheel teeth, the magnetic flux set up by magnet (3) undergoes fluctuations due to changes in the gap. These fluctuations set up an electromotive force in winding (2) and a voltage is set up at the terminals that is alternatively positive (tooth facing sensor) and negative (gap facing sensor). Rpm sensor peak output voltage depends, all else being equal, on the distance between the sensor and the phonic wheel teeth (gap). The sensor gap angular position cannot be adjusted. Sensor resistance may be measured by disconnecting the connector and connecting an ohmmeter at the sensor terminals. The frequency and amplitude of the signal are proportional to the engine rotation speed. Us - induced voltage a - 58 periods b - corresponds to 1 complete revolution of the crankshaft t - time Sensor specifications: Resistance: from 300 to 400 ohm Gap 1mm ± 0.5 (not adjustable) Ring gear specifications: 60-2=58 teeth (1 tooth corresponds to 6° of the crankshaft). Motorized throttle The throttle casing incorporates several ignition system components. 1 - Throttle 2 - Motor 3 - Twin track throttle potentiometer 4 - Intake air temperature sensor 5 - Idler gears 6 - Fuel vapour reicrulation pipe from canister 7 - Oil vapour reicrulation pipe from engine The opening of the throttle is not managed directly through the cable operated by the accelerator pedal but by means of an electrical signal coming from the accelerator pedal potentiometer. This allows the NCM to manage any requests coming from other nodes at the same time: climate control node, Brake Node, Cruise Control, Automatic Transmission Node, etc. The position of the throttle is determined by the motor on the throttle casing which is, in turn, managed by the NCM. A twin track potentiometer positioned on the throttle axis allows the NCM to recognize the position with precision; this potentiometer cannot be adjusted. This information is used to recognize foot raised or end of travel conditions. Faults that can be detected Engine no longer operated (open circuit or short circuit) The NCM receive two conflicting pieces of electrical information: accelerator pedal position (from the accelerator potentiometer), throttle position (from the throttle potentiometer). The throttle is in the rest position. This position is not the position that relates to the engine idle speed which, in the case of the motorized throttle, corresponds to a throttle opening of around 8° . Q - air flow rate in kg/h %agr; - throttle opening angle in degrees With the motor not supplied, the throttle finds itself in the mechanical closed position which, in effect, corresponds to the rest position. In this position, thanks to the shape of the throttle casing, the air flow rate is around 8 times higher than the minimum. The NCM manages the fuel flow rate and the ignition advance according to the position of the accelerator pedal. Engine permanently operated The NCM receive two conflicting pieces of electrical information: accelerator pedal position (from the accelerator potentiometer), throttle position (from the throttle potentiometer). The throttle is in the maximum opening position. The NCM manages the fuel flow rate and the ignition advance according to the position of the accelerator pedal restricting the engine speed to 1500 rpm. The NCM continuously checks the information relating to the throttle potentiomter and to the pressure sensor. This check makes it possible to check the consistency of the throttle position in relation to the engine rotation speed. In this case the NCM adopts strategies aimed to reduce engine performance and communicates the failure status by lighting up the diagnostic warning light. One of the two potentiometer tracks defective (short circuit or open circuit) The NCM considers the information coming from the track that is working properly. In this case the NCM adopts strategies aimed to reduce engine performance and communicates the failure status by lighting up the diagnostic warning light. Self-learning procedure The self-learning procedure consists of causing the NCM to recognize the motorized throttle closed and maximum opening positions; this is done in the following cases: replacement of the NCM, replacement of the throttle casing, repair of the throttle casing following the detection of a fault. To carry out the procedure: start the engine, carry out an initilization cycle for the self-adjustment parameters, during this stage the NCM reads the self-adjustment parameters in the EEPROM, stop the engine, the power latch sequence is launched, wait until the end of the power latch sequence (10 minutes max.), at the end of this sequence the throttle will be placed in the maximum opening position, then in the rest position, place the key in the ON position, wait until any errors are zeroed, start the engine without accelerating and let it idle for two minutes, during the first 4 seconds the NCM will record the accelerator pedal potentiometer idle position. The consequence of not applying the self-learning procedure Not following the self-learning procedure does not allow the NCM to manage the operation of the engine correctly; in this case there could be damage to the motorized throttle because the NCM does not recognize the maximum opening and closing positions. However, after the engine is switched off for the first time, the NCM automatically carries out the self-learning procedure during the power latch procedure (placing the throttle in the maximum opening position and then in the closed position). During normal use of the vehicle the NCM carries out these self-learning cycles regularly to update the values recorded in the EEPROM. Accelerator potentiometer The accelerator potentiometer is located in the engine compartment and is connected to the accelerator pedal by a cable. The potentiometer receives a 5V supply from the NCM to which it transmits a voltage which varies according to the position of the pedal. This signal is managed by the NCM in the same way as the signals from the following nodes: Climate Control Node, Automatic Transmission Node, Brake Node, Cruise Control When the engine is started, the opening of the throttle is pre-programmed to a certain position irrespective of the position of the accelerator pedal. Self-learning procedure The self-learning procedure consists of making the NCM recognize the potentiometer rest position (corresponding to the rest position of the pedal), the pedal end of travel position is automatically calculated from the rest position. The self-learning procedure is carried out in the following cases: replacement of the NCM, replacement of the accelerator pedal potentiometer, repair of the accelerator pedal following the detection of a fault, reprogramming of the NCM. Potentiometer self-learning procedure if the NCM is being reprogrammed After reprogramming, wait for 5 seconds before turning the key to the OFF position, during these 5 seconds the NCM will carry out the position learning procedure for the motorized throttle: keep the key in the OFF position for 5 seconds, during these 5 seconds the NCM will memorize the new data in the EEPROM and re-establish communication with the NBC; start the engine without accelerating and let it idle for two minutes (start the engine with the temperature of the coolant below 60°C), during the first 4 seconds the NCM will record the accelerator pedal potentiometer idle position. Potentiometer self-learning procedure if a component is being replaced The components involved are: NCM, throttle body, accelerator pedal potentiometer, Lambda sensors, any component should be replaced with the ignition switched off. To carry out the procedure: start the engine, carry out an initilization cycle for the self-adjustment parameters, during this stage the NCM reads the self-adjustment parameters in the EEPROM, stop the engine, the power latch sequence is launched, wait until the end of the power latch sequence (10 minutes max.), at the end of this sequence the throttle will be placed in the maximum opening position, then in the rest position, place the key in the ON position, wait until any errors are zeroed, start the engine without accelerating and let it idle for two minutes, during the first 4 seconds the NCM will record the accelerator pedal potentiometer idle position. The consequence of not applying the self-learning procedure Not following the self-learning procedures does not allow the NCM to manage the operation of the engine correctly. Phase transformer solenoid valve The solenoid valve which manages the phase transformer is located on the monobloc, timing side and receives a 12V supply and is controlled by the engine management node being earthed. The NCM operates the solenoid valve in the following conditions: engine speed below 4300 rpm, high engine torque, oil temperature between 40°C and 140°C. When the solenoid valve is activated, the pressurized oil, coming from the lubrication circuit, is channelled into the camshaft operating system rotating it through 20°. For the correct management of the solenoid valve, the NCM needs to know the temperature of the engine oil, in effect, below 40°C and above 140°C the density of the oil does not allow the NCM to operate the solenoid valve correctly. The temperature of the engine oil is calculated starting with that of the engine coolant. In effect, the oil temperature sensor, on the oil sump, detects a different temperature from that on the monobloc, whilst conversely the temperature of the coolant is very close to that of the oil. The calculation of the temperature of the oil is carried out using parameters that take the different specifications of the two fluids into account. Absolute pressure sensor The pressure sensor continuously detects the pressure of the air in the intake manifold. The pressure sensor is the piezoresistive type. The sensitive element consists of a resistive bridge serigraphed on a flexible diaphragm which separates the measuring chamber (connected to the inlet manifold) and the reference chamber (in which the vacuum has been created). Receiving a 5V supply from the control unit, this sensor provides an output voltage proportional to the absolute pressure measured. This information, transmitted to the Engine Management Node, makes it possible to: calculate the mass of air introduced into the engine (using the engine speed and air temperature parameters), adapt the fuel flow rate injected according to variations in the engine load and atmospheric pressure, vary the ignition advance. The variation in altitude is used to calaculate the injection times; in effect, the mass of intake air varies according to: atmospheric pressure (consequently altitude), air temperature, engine speed. The measurements are taken: each time the engine is started, at high engine load and low speed conditions (climbing a hill, change in altitude and atmospheric pressure). Engine timing sensor The engine timing sensor, together with the engine speed and TDC signal, allows the control unit to recognise cylinder sequence when implementing phased injection. This signal is generated by a Hall-effect sensor fitted near the exhaust camshaft. The sensor angular position cannot be adjusted. The sensor information makes it possible to: phase the injection and ignition coils sequentially, decrease the ignition advance to reduce knocking. The sensor receives a 5V supply and provides a signal that can be directly used by the Engine Management Node. Knock sensor This piezoelectric sensor is fitted on the engine block in a symmetrical position in relation to cylinder pairs 1-2 and 3-4. This positioning is determined by the need to detect the onset of knock in a similar way for all cylinders. This sensor is used to measure knock, a vibration effect caused by irregular mixture combustion in the combustion chamber. If repeated, this effect may harm mechanical parts due to an anomalous temperature increase in the walls. The sensor provides a voltage proportional to the vibrations detected. If there is detonation, the NCM reduces the ignition advance between 2° and 12°, then restores normal conditions later on. Parallel to the variation in the advance, the NCM manages the enrichment of the air/fuel mixture to prevent an increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases. It consists of a plastic case with the actual resistance element fitted at one end. This takes the form of an NTC thermistor (Negative Temperature Coefficient - i.e. the sensor electrical resistance falls as temperature rises). The reference voltage is 5V. Because the control unit input circuit is designed as a voltage divider, this voltage is distributed between a resistance present in the control unit and the sensor NTC resistance. The control unit is therefore able to assess sensor resistance changes via changes in the voltage and thus obtain temperature information. The graph shows the sensor specification curve, which may be measured by disconnecting the connector and connecting an ohmmeter to the sensor terminals. Coolant temperature sensor The sensor is installed on the thermostat body. It consists of a brass case that acts as the actual resistance element. It takes the form of an NTC thermistor (Negative Temperature Coefficient - i.e. the sensor electrical resistance falls as temperature rises). 1 - Sensor connector 2 - NTC pad housing The reference voltage is 5V. Because the control unit input circuit is designed as a voltage divider, this voltage is distributed between a resistance present in the control unit and the sensor NTC resistance. The control unit is therefore able to assess sensor resistance changes via changes in the voltage and thus obtain temperature information. The graph shows the sensor specification curve, which may be measured by disconnecting the connector and connecting an ohmmeter to the sensor terminals. Ignition coils The ignition circuit is the inductive discharge, static advance type where the high tension is supplied by two twin output coils incorporated in a single element and fitted directly above the spark plugs (no high tension leads). In this type of coil the current at the secondary winding (discharge current) always has the same polarity: therefore one circuit terminal is positive and the other negative. This means that the discharge current in the secondary winding always flows in the same direction and therefore the sparks for the two cylinders connected to the coil strike in the opposite way: in the spark plug with the positive centre electrode the spark strikes from the earth electrode to the centre electrode; in the spark plug with the negative centre electrode the spark strikes from the centre electrode to the earth electrode; As a result, the wear of the electrodes in the two spark plugs is different. Since the intensity of the spark depends on the resistance between the electrodes (dielectric), the following two conditions occur: in the cylinder in the crossover stage the spark is weak (lost spark) as a result of almost atmospheric pressure in the actual cylinder in the cylinder at the end of the compression stroke the spark is intense (useful spark) as a result of the high pressure in the combustion chamber. The advance is controlled by the NCM in accordance with a set map based on the following parameter: engine speed, inlet pressure. Power steering pressure switch This sensor, fitted on the pump high pressure outlet pipe, consists of a pressure switch that closes when the hydraulic pressure exceeds a certain level (around 35 bar) corresponding to the steering almost in the end of travel position: this information is used to manage the idle speed control actuator in advance of power absorption (by the power assisted steering pump) due to steering. Injectors The injectors have the task of supplying the amount of fuel required for the operation of the engine: the fuel is injected into the intake manifold immediately upstream of the inlet valves. The injectors are the twin jet, top-feed type with the top of the casing also housing the electrical winding connected to the connector (3) terminals. The injectors receive a 12V supply and are operated by being earthed. The NCM controls the injectors separately when the inlet valves are closed in the following order: 1, 3, 4, 2. When the current passes through the winding, the magnetic field created attracts the shutter opening the injector and causing the flow of fuel. There are two seals, one of the fuel manifold side (1) and one on the intake manifold side (2). A tooth (4) determines the angular position of the injector in relation to the intake manifold to ensure that the jets are correctly directed in relation to the inlet valves. Injector resistance is around 14.5 ohm and may be measured by disconnecting the connector and connecting an ohmmeter as shown in the figure. The quantity of fuel injected depends on the injector opening time (injection time). Fuel drip tray assembly Fuel pump The pump is housed inside the fuel tank on a special drip tray which also supports the level gauge and is fitted with a filter on the pump inlet. The pressure regulator is also fitted on the pump supply. The pump is the single stage, peripheral flow type and is designed to run on unleaded petrol. The rotor is driven by a direct current electric motor supplied by a relay operated by the control unit to ensure: the pump cuts out if the engine speed goes below a certain level; the timed operation (around 5 seconds) each time the ignition is turned to the ON position, even if the engine is not started up operation with the engine started. The pump is equipped with an excess pressure valve that short circuits the supply if the pressure in the supply circuit exceeds around 5 bar to prevent the electric motor from overheating. In addition, the pressure regulator prevents the entire fuel circuit from draining when the pump is not working, maintaining a residual pressure in the circuit for a certain length of time. Fuel pressure regulator This is a device located in the top of the drip tray. The function of the regulator is to: keep the supply pressure constant in all engine operating conditions, maintain a residual pressure for a pre-set period, after the engine switches off, to facilitate starting the engine when warm, preventing the formation of fuel vapours inside the supply circuit. The pressure regulator is calibrated in the factory to maintain a residual pressure of 3.50 bar. 1 - pressure regulator Fuel filter The filter, fitted on the supply pipe is located near the tank and comprises an aluminium outer casing and an internal element made from special paper with a high filtering capacity that traps impurities up to 8 microns in diameter. 1 - Arrow showing fitting direction; 2 - Fuel inlet from the tank; 3- Fuel outlet to the manifold. When fitting the filter, pay attention to the direction of the arrow on the actual filter. Twin relay The twin relay comprises: a main relay (A); a power relay (B); The main relay (A) supplies the following components: With the ignition switch turned off: no supply. With the ignition switch turned on or with the engine running: engine management control unit (1) power relay (B). After the ignition switch has been turned off: the Engine Management Node for a defined period (power latch) in order to: reposition the idle speed adjustment actuator and facilitate post-starting when warm, manage the engine cooling, carrying out the self-learning of the motorized throttle minimum and maximum opening positions. The power relay (B) supplies the following components. With the ignition switch turned off: no supply. With the ignition switch turned on or with the engine running: ignition coil (2); carbon filter scrubbing solenoid valve (3); throttle casing heater (4); injectors (5); fuel pump (6); Lambda sensor heaters (7); EGR solenoid valve (8). The supply is maintained for 2 to 3 seconds, then interrupted if the engine is not started (no engine speed signal) or if the speed goes below a minimum level. After the ignition is switched off: no supply. Activated charcoal filter The active charcoal filter is fitted under the bodyshell. It consists of carbon granules that trap fuel vapours entering intake (2). Warm flushing air enters intake (4) and flows over the carbon granules to remove fuel vapours and carry them towards outlet (3) and then on to the cut-off valve. Air entering intake (4) may also be drawn in by the vacuum in the tank to ventilate the tank. 1 - Carbon filter 2 - Vapour inlet (from the tank) 3 - Vapour oulet (to the manifold) 4 - Scrubbing air intake Active charcoal filter scrubbing solenoid The charcoal filter scrubbing solenoid valve is located between the active charcoal filter and the throttle casing. This valve, the normally closed type, is operated by the NCM at 12V in duty-cycle allowing the recirculation of the fuel vapours contained in the charcoal filter, thereby controlling the flow reaching the intake manifold. Lambda sensors The Lambda sensors measure exhaust gas oxygen content: one is fitted on the exhaust pipe upstream of the catalytic silencer, the other downstream of the catalyzer. Lambda = 1 Ideal mixture (stoichiometric) Lambda > 1 Lean mixture Excess air; CO level tends to be low lambda < 1 rich mixture Lack of air; CO level tends to be high Resistance: 4,5 ± 0.5 Ohm at 20° C The sensor output signal is sent to the NCM for retroactive correction (feedback) of the mixture concentration. When the sensor supplies a low signal (voltage lower than 200 mV), the control unit detects a lean mixture and increases injection time. Then when the sensor signal is high (voltage higher than 800 mV), the control unit detects a rich mixture and decreases injection time. This event sequence is repeated with a frequency in the order of tens of Hertz to ensure that the engine runs on a mixture that fluctuates constantly about a stioichiometric level. At temperatures lower than 300° C, the ceramic material is inactive and the sensor cannot therefore send reliable signals: the sensor is fitted with an electrical heater coil to ensure fast heat at start-up and maintain a minimum temperature. During certain engine operating stages the NCM does not take the Lambda sensor signal into account, namely: with the engine cold (temperature below 20°C), engine operating at high speed. The downstream sensor is identical to the upstream sensor. Sensors can be quickly be put out of service by the presence of even small amounts of lead in the fuel. Sensor heater resistances may be measured by disconnecting the connector and connecting an ohmmeter as shown in the figure. Catalytic silencer The catalytic converter is a device that can remove the three main polluting compounds present in exhaust gases simultaneously: unburnt hydrocarbons (HC), carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen oxides (NOx). Two types of chemical reaction take place inside the converter: oxidation of CO and HC to carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O); reduction of NQx to nitrogen (N2). This reactions can take place very quickly due to the presence of a layer of active substances (platinum and rhodium) inside the converter structure (ceramic mount) that accelerate the conversion rate of harmful substances enormously. The efficiency of this conversion process is affected by the fact that the concentration of the mixture on which the engine runs fluctuates continuously about a stoichiometric level. This is achieved by the feedback control exercised by the control unit on the basis of signals from the lambda sensor. Lastly, the conversion processes are activated at temperatures in excess of 300 - 350° C (the optimum temperature is between 600° and 800°C): it is therefore essential for the catalytic converter to reach this temperature as quickly as possible so that it can work correctly. Temperatures around 1000°C lead to rapid damage of the catalyzer; a correct air/fuel mixture together with precisely calculated ignition times keep the catalyzer at the ideal operating temperature. When working near the catalytic converter, leave the vehicle to stand for a while because the internal working temperature of the catalytic converter is between 500° and 850° C. The internal part of the catalytic converter can essentially be put out of service by two causes: presence of lead in the fuel that lowers conversion levels to practically zero (lead contamination) and also irreparably damages the lambda sensor; presence of totally unburnt fuel in the exhaust gas due to misfiring that brings about a temperature increase sufficient to melt the mount. 1 - External case in steel 2 - Thermal insulation 3 - One-piece ceramic structure Exhaust air injection system The exhaust air injection system consists of the following elements: Electric air pump Supply relay Cut out valve Exhaust manifold Air pump relay The relay receives a 12V supply and is operated by the NCM, it is designed to supply the exhaut air injection pump. The NCM controls the relay: for around 10 seconds at temperatures below -7°C, to prevent the pump and the cut out valve from seizing, for around 30 seconds at temperatures between -7°C and 15°C, to prevent the pump and the cut out valve from seizing, for around 80 seconds at temperatures between 15°C and 80°C, with around 20% enrichment of the mixture. The relay is activated when the engine is started and during idling and is no longer operated at speeds above 2500 rpm. Air pump The electric air pump is located in the engine compartment and is operated by the NCM through the activation of the relay with a flow rate of around 20 kg/h. The pump blows air through the exhaust manifold upstream of the catalyzer, this operation gives rise to post-combustion. The post-combustion increases the temperature of the exhaust gases helping the catalyzer to reach optimum operation more quickly. Cut out valve This is located in the air injection circuit between the air pump and the exhaust manifold and has the following functions: to insulate the air injection circuit when the air pump is not working, preventing the intake of gases by the exhaust manifold; ensuring the immediate cut out of air injection when the pump is no longer supplied. When the air pump is activated, the pressure in the pipe reaches the upper capsule and overcomes the resistance of the spring, opening the valve. As soon as the pump is deactivated, the pressure is reduced and the spring recalles the valve, closing it. The regeneration of the filter depends on the temperature of the exhaust gases and is activated beyond the particle combustion level (around 450°C if the additive function is present). There are two types of regeneration: natural regeneration, artificial regeneration. Natural regeneration When the temperature of the exhaust gases approaches the regeneration level (with the additive function around 450 °C), the particles burn naturally inside the filter. In this case no intervention is required by the engine management node. Driving conditions directly affect the temperature of the exhaust gases and, consequently, the temperature inside the filter. Artificial regeneration Artificial regeneration is managed by the engine management node by means of commands designed to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases until the particle combustion level is reached. Artificial regeneration involves two stages: stage 1: increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter, stage 2: increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases. The engine management node manages the change from the first stage to the second stage according to the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter; this change is not permitted until the first stage has been activated for a certain period or the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter have reached pre-set values. Each time the artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node: interrupts the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR); operates the turbine to keep the engine torque constant, if necessary, controls the opening of the valve for heating the intake air (through the reversal of the position of the two control valves), activates post-injection (which heats the exhaust gases directly), requests the activation of several electrical consumers. Artificial regeneration - first stage When first stage artificial regeneration is required, the engine management node adapts the post-injection strategies to increase the temperature of the catalytic converter. 1 - pilot injection 2 - main injection 3 - first post-injection period 4 - post-injection Post-injection takes place immediately after the main injection which makes it possible to increase the temperature of the exhaust gases through combustion in the cylinder after top dead centre. This stage ensures an increase in the temperature of the catalytic converter until the maximum efficiency level is reached. By comparing the temperature of the exhaust gases upstream and downstream of the catalytic converter, the engine management node uses its internal strategy to determine whether the catalytic converter has reached its maximum conversion level; when this level is reached, it activates the second artificial regeneration stage. Artificial regeneration - second stage At the end of the first artificial regeneration stage, the engine management node implements strategies that allow a further increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases (second stage). 1 - pilot injection 2 - main injection 3 - first post-injection period 4 - post-injection The period that separates the main injection from the post-injection is longer than for the first stage, the post-injection period is longer and is divided into two parts: the first allows the temperature of the exhaust gases to be kept high, the second allows the hydrocarbons (HC) required for post-combustion to be supplied to the catalytic converter. Artificial regeneration activation conditions Before activating the artificial regeneration strategies, the engine management node checks that: the temperature of the engine coolant is ³ 60°C, the engine speed is equal to a pre-set level, artificial regeneration is inhibited during idling, the vehicle has travelled at least 280 km since the last regeneration. The filter blockage level due to particles is controlled by means of two parameters: the mileage between each regeneration (N1), differential pressure (?Pn). Counting the distance travelled The information relating the distance travelled since the last regeneration (calculatd by the engine management node), makes it possible to activate the artificial regeneration independently of the information supplied by the differential pressure sensor. This strategy makes it possible to limit the mass of particles to be burnt by the filter since the combustion of a high level of particles could increase the temperature of the filter too much causing it to be ruined. The engine managment node activates artificial regeneration strategies when the distance travelled since the last regeneration reaches a pre-set value, which varies according to the aging of the filter (quantity of cerium oxide accumulated). f - regeneration frequency (expressed in km) km - total mileage N - aging of the filter (total mileage for the filter), N2 - mileage determining the activation of the regeneration when N1 (mileage since the last regeneration) ³ N2 the engine management node establishes the start and the duration of a period of time (T2) during which post-injection takes place. Differential pressure sensor signal The signal from the differential pressure sensor activates the artificial regeneration strategies independently of the mileage since the last regeneration. To stop artificial regeneration activated by the differential pressure signal: the filter operating zone must be lower than the initial level, the period during which post-injection takes place (established by the engine management node) must have elapsed. The temperature of the exhaust gases gradually increases until the regeneration level is reached. The capacity, duration and time of the start of post-injection are determined by strategies that take the engine operating conditions and the level of assistance required into account. Engine torque When engine speed and load conditions are constant, post-injection produces an increase in engine torque. To maintain the same driving conditions and prevent a variation in engine torque, the engine management node: the switching on of the heated rear windscreen, the switching on of the radiator cooling fan at low speed, the switching on of the radiator cooling fan at medium speed, the switching on of the heater plugs. Activation of the high pressure pump third piston During artificial regeneration the high pressure pump third piston is also activ ated to ensure the correct fuel flow rate required for post-injection. Activation of electrical consumers The activation of electrical consumers causes the engagement of the alternator and, as a result, an increase in resistant torque. This situation facilitates an increase in the temperature of the exhaust gases. Regulation of the intake air heating circuit Each time artificial regeneration is activated, the engine management node keeps the throttle valve on the air/water heater duce open and closes the one of the intercooler duct in order to force the flow of air inside the actual heater.

GENERAL SPECIFICATIONS In conventional electrical systems, functions are activated with the aid of dedicated point-to-point lines The increase in the number of electrical/electronic devices on board new cars has given rise to heavier and more complex connections. This is partly due to the complexity of the functions implemented in the burgeoning number of electronic units - which also need to exchange data continually: all this makes new electrical systems more difficult to install and increases the complexity of fault diagnosis. Many problems have been overcome and new electrical systems have been optimised compared to conventional systems by using a network form of connection. This provides a more effective means of managing communication on the board the car and of transferring data between the various subsystems. Information is distributed via serial pathways (buses) that may take the form of: individual wires, twisted wire pairs or even optical fibres. Conventional solution The three control units (electronic nodes) require a number (N) of wires for each input/output data item in order to perform their function. This multiplied the amount of cable required to the point that systems are made more complex (design and manufacture) and more voluminous (weight, bulk, cost). Some 40 kg of wiring looms are required that stretch for more than 2 km - and this figure could double every 10 years because even now a car could be equipped wiht 20 to 40 electronic control units (ECUs). Tx - information to be transmitted from nodes A (A1,A2) B (B1, B2) C (C1, C2) Rx - information to be received from nodes A (B1, B2, C1) B (A1, A2, C2) C (A2, B1, B2) The first step towards reducing the volume and complexity of wiring looms was to group several electronic functions in a single unit: fewer control units = fewer wires. Examples of integation Engine control unit (NCM) manages: injection, ignition, pollution system, engine cooling control etc. 1 - Engine management control unit 2 - Engine cooling fan, 1st speed 3 - Engine cooling fan, 2nd speed 4 - Injectors (injection) 5 - Coils (ignition) 6 - Lambda sensor Integration of electrical/electronic functions in a single electronic control unit (ECU) has allowed us to improve: current uptake management (lower battery wear); operation of appliances, because they are managed by a single control unit; troubleshootng due to self-diagnostic functions in the control units. This first stage allowed us to reduce the number of electronic units but not to reduce the volume of wiring to a sufficient extent. MULTIPLEXING solution This involves exchanging various data signals between various ECUs on a single transmission channel (a principle already used for phone, radio and TV networks): 1 BUS (2 wires) for all data. The second stage allowed us to make a decise leap in terms of: Reducing and simplifying the wiring Reducing the number of sensors (information sharing) Allowing ECUs to communicate among themselves. As more and more systems require interconnection, the MULTIPLEXING solution becomes more and more attractive. In general terms, in order to transmit data via a multiplexing system we need to define the following with precision: transmission channel (wires, optical fibres, radio waves etc.); type of signal sent via the channel (voltage, current, light etc.); the communication protocol (all the rules that allow management of analogue or digital transmission type, code type, address, transmission order, error detection etc.). The transmission support or channel on the car is a pair of wires known as a BUS. The system therefore transmits batches (packages of information sent one after another. This is not done in any particular set order but in accordance with the needs of the control unit). The following protocols are used for the voltage signals produced; CAN protocol (Controller Area Network): used for the high speed transfer of data (engine management, ABS, automatic transmission) initiated and developed by Rober Bosch as early as 1983, VAN protocol: used for managing standard bodywork functions. Binary The language of the electronic units is binary - compatible with the electronic circuits (high low) (open closed etc.): to transmit information, data must therefore be handled in accordance with specific codes. Various codes have therefore been developed to meet all requirements. One of the most common codes is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange). This alphanumerical code uses coded groups of bits. It is able to represent the 26 letters of the English alphabet plus the ten decimal numbers in addition to punctuation marks and instruction commands. ASCII is an eight bit binary code. Seven bits are used to code information and the eighth is used to check errors. By using seven bits per character, it is posible to code no fewer than 128 information including decimal numbers, upper and lower case letters of the alphabet, punctuation marks etc. Once the number of bits making up a word (i.e. the word length) has been fixed by a data code, this number must not be altered. A group of eight bits is called a byte and represents 256 values: this number is obtained by testing all possible combinations of (0) and (1) in the eight positions availalbe per byte, for example 00000001, 00001111, 11111111 etc. The number 256 (2 exp. 8) can be used to represent the set of alphabetical characters, punctuation marks, accented or special characters etc. In effect, therefore, a single byte may represent a number, a letter of the alphabet, a punctuation mark or a special character. The byte is used as a unit of measurement in saved data quantities and memory device storage capacity. As with any unit of measurement, bytes are also defined as multiple amounts: 1 kilobyte (kb) = 1024 bytes = 2 exp. 10 (2 < sup > 10 < /sup > ) 1 megabyte (Mb) = 1024 kb (about one million bytes) = 2 exp. 20 (2 < sup > 20 < /sup > ) 1 gigabyte (Mb) = 1024 kb (about one billion bytes) = 2 exp. 30 (2 < sup > 30 < /sup > ) 1 terabyte (Mb) = 1024 Gb (about one trillion bytes) = 2 exp. 40 (2 < sup > 40 < /sup > ) Analogue "Linear" electronics is the term applied to analogue effects, i.e. effects that are proportional and continuous. A water tap is an example of an analogue switch. This is because it can used to shut off the water flow completely, turn the flow to maximum and also obtain all the other intermediate positions that occur on the continuum between the closed state and the fully open state. The Tester mobile coil instrument is also analogue: the pointer may indicate the measurement position from zero to full scale deflection, by moving continuously along the entire graduated scale and passing through all the points on its way. Digital Digital electronic, on the other hand, denotes progress by discrete quantities in quantifiable steps. A light switch is an example of digital operation because the only possible statuses are well-defined and distinct. In this case there are two: on and off, with no intermediate positions. In practice, a digital gauge (whether it operates using warning lights or numbers) increases in steps. It is not possible to determine, for example, the exact level of a fluid between a stage when one warning light on the level gauge is lit and the next is still turned off. The sensitivity is therefore one step, i.e. the interval between one warning light and the next. The reading is, however, precise and non-subjective. It is possible to interpose a series of steps between one warning light and the next containing an equal number of warning lights and so on until the discrete measurement steps can practically be equated with the continuous line of an analogue instrument. The similarity is, however, more apparent than real because each step on the digital guage, however small, determines a well-defined position and represents an unequivocable value. Above all, it is not subject to parallalax or interpolation reading errors. To sum up, the sensitivity of a digital instrument is equivalent to that of an analogue instrument but the reading accuracy is always higher. OPERATION OF MULTIPLEXING NETWORK The designer of the multiplex system allocated control functions to the Body Computer. The additional Body Computer functions allow it to provide information on: network activities status; operational failure status of individual electronic units (nodes); a possible network fault. The Body Computer Node is given the task of "waking up" the network when the ignition key is turned on. In the case of a fault in the NBC, the Instrument Panel Node (NQS) is given the task of waking up the network. The NQS cuts in only if it is not woken up by the Body Computer after a certain length of time with the ignition key. This prevents network conflicts. All the the "Node" electronic units process the various signals from associated sensors for individual management purposes and also to manage other control units. On latest-generation electrical systems, the number of electronic unit that are interconnected, and thus the number of data packages that need to be handled, is very high. For this reason, one or more (CAN or VAN type) networks are used in these systems. Compared to conventional wiring, these allow more effective information exchange between the various electronic units. The physical means used for the network (either VAN or CAN) is a twin plaited copper wire cable; where one of the wires is for high voltage and the other low voltage. The BUS signals are differential, i.e. the value allocated to the bits is represented by the difference between voltage levels. To sum up, the combined use of two wires and differential signals allow data packages to be exchanged between different control units on the network. This is even possible in the presence of electromagnetic interference. Transmission and exchange of data between the VAN and CAN and the transfer of data between the lower speed network and the high speed network and vice versa takes place in the Body Computer node (gateway function). The message issued to a network by an electronic unit or node is known as a "raster" (data package). It takes the form of a series of pulses, as mentioned previously (known as bits) that take the value (1) or (0). This denotes the presence of absence of a transmitted signal. Communication protocol Circulation or transmission of a message known as a frame or data package on a multiplexing network is possible only if a transmission protocol is adopted. This the set of rules that allows the exchange of data and controls between two or more electronic units (control units or, better still, nodes). FRAME FORMAT 1 - Frame 2 - Blocks A - Identifies the beginning of transmission or start of a new frame (START OF FRAME. SOF) consists of 1 dominant bit and indicates to all other interfaced nodes that they must synchronise with this SOF bit (awake the BUS that may be in stand by). B - Identifier (12 bits): marks and identifies the contents of the message. Also contains information on message recipients. Arbitrage of transmitted frames is carried out in this field. This means that the indentifier code allows frame content and priority allocated by the network architect to be uniquely identified. C - Control range (4 bits); indicates the nature of the frame or message and makes it possible to indicate whether the frame is a question, a response or data diffusion. At the same time it indicates whether it is necessary for the frame recipient to communicate that the frame has been correctly received. D - Data to be trasmitted (may be orders or information to be transmitted): for the VAN it can be between 0 and 28 bytes (1 byte = 8 bits), whilst for the CAN it can be between 0 and 8 bytes. E - Control field; allows a check to be run that the data transmitted are unaltered (message validity). The node or nodes that detect the presence of an error first issue a series of dominant warning bits. The transmitting node eliminates the message and emits a new frame after a certain time lapse. F- Reception confirmation. This allows all the destination nodes to indicate that the frame has been correctly transmitted. For messages transmitted via the VAN, confirmation of receipt is optional, whilst for frames transmitted via the CAN it is compulsory. G - End of frame: determines the end of the message with no ambiguity. Bus communication rules The two types of nodes There are two different types of nodes: Master Node: issues frames to send or receive information, receives frames sent directly to its address or diffused over the network without a particular destination; Slave Node: receives frames and only issues them if interrogated directly In the following type of network: Master / Slave, the management of the information is entrusted solely to the Master Node, In the following type of network: Multi Master, the management of the information is not concentrated at a single Node, but they are all authorized to circulate messages. In a mixed type of network: different Master Nodes with Slave Nodes, the information is managed by the Master nodes. Priority management (Superimposition or collision of non-destructive frame) The system protocol allows superimposition problems to be handled when several nodes need to emit a frame simultaneously. Each node possesses an identification code that also expresses its priority. In practice, when a node expresses its intention to transmit a frame on the network by means of its initial bit and another node simultaneously carries out the same operation, because both read (as well as transmit) the signals emitted by the network, the node that detects a difference between the emitted signal and the received signal detects that another node is emitting a higher priority frame. The node that transmits the lower priority message immediately interrupts its transmission and makes way for the node that is transmitting a higher priority message. In practice, the high priority message is sent to the network without any interruption or delay. Naturally, the nodes that intended to transmit messages with lower priority must suspend transmission to become receivers and then re-attempt to send the frame when transmission is complete. This non-destructive superimposition is regulated by bit arbitrage. One bit is called the dominant bit and allocated a value of zero (0) while the other bit is known as a recessive bit and its value is equal to one (1). The higher priority frame gains the right to be transmitted on the BUS. A dominant level (0) always takes precedence over a recessive level (1). Types of information interchange Communication between the various nodes can be: point to point: sending the data involves a precise destination, diffused: the data transmitted does not have a precise destination question / response: the answer may be provided directly within the question frame or in a different frame dedicated to the response. with the confirmation of receipt: the node that receives the frame completes the actual frame on receipt. Structure of the network The physical medium used for automotive networks is double copper electrical cable type, where one wire is associated with a higher voltage level than the other. In order to transfer and receive information, all electrical/electronic units are connected to the network by means of switching interfaces built into the electronic units that are known as transceivers. The electronic units in the networks are programmed and operate by means of data and information storage, processing and transmission using a binary convention, i.e. two symbols that denote two basic electrical logic statuses. absence of voltage, circuit open or level zero (0) presence of voltage; circult closed; or level one (1) levels (0) and (1) constitute the basic information unit known as a BIT (binary digit) High transmission speed CAN The CAN is illustrated below 1 - Node 1 2 - Node 2 3 - Node n The network displays the following characteristics: BUS comprising 2 twisted copper wires 0.6 mm² in diametro, differential voltage signals on the two lines known as CAN H and CAN L, the electrical signal is transmitted opposite, transmission sped of 250 kbit/sec, termination resistances at the NBC and NCM nodes (60 O), each node is capable of generating a differential voltage of between 1.5 V and 3.5 V measured on a resistance load of 60 Ohms, there can be a maximum of 30 nodes. To limit electrical current consumption, the electronic circuitry of the various nodes is no longer supplied one minute after the engine has been switched off and the ignition key extracted from the ignition. However, several functions can wake the system up again (e.g. opening the doors). STRUCTURE The system interacts with all electrical system functions to directly control body functions (visibility, access, on-board information, comfort, communications etc.) and supports information exchange between traction control systems (engine, braking, gearbox etc.). Power is distributed via the junction units and/or fuse boxes. These are connected to control elements (relays and static actuators) to ensure maximum electrical protection and minimum complexity. Systems of this type offer innumerable benenfits, for example: sensors included in the various subsystems are available to the network; information may be shared; sensor duplication is eliminated; system flexibility is increased; new functions may be added simply by changing the software (developments throughout the car's lifetime), wiring design is simplified and the number of connectors reduced, the operational safety of electronic devices is increased to improve the reliability of information transmitted, because a diagnostic function is built-in, service operations on electric/electronic components are easier. Network architecture The structure consists of four communication networks which connect nodes belonging to the different areas (vehicle dynamic control and bodywork functions) and a certain number of complementary serial lines used for diagnosis and other specific functions: a multi-master type CAN for the dynamic control of the vehicle (high speed), a multi-master type VAN known as a COMFORT network which connects the NBC to the information or comfort equipment. a master/slave type VAN divided into two sub sectors also known as BODYWORK networks: the VAN CAR1 and the VAN CAR2.
